headlines.article_text: Home Depot (HD) Q3 earnings 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Home Depot named Richard McPhail as its new CEO effective next week. McPhail currently serves as CFO. CEO Ted Decker had been on a temporary medical leave of absence but has since returned, according to Home Depot. The company made the announcement as it posted earnings and revenue that beat expectations. In this article HD Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Home Depot store logo sign is seen in Chicago, Illinois, United States, on August 3, 2026. Marcin Golba | Nurphoto | Getty Images Home Depot on Tuesday announced its Chief Financial Officer Richard McPhail will become CEO of the company, replacing Ted Decker, effective next week. Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot said Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to replace McPhail. Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said. "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession plan." McPhail has been with the company since 2005, holding multiple executive roles. "We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick. He said the company will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using AI tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market. Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the company has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects. Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results. The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company said comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount. Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.86 adjusted vs. $3.84 expected Revenue: $43.4 billion vs. $42.80 billion expected The company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86. Revenue rose 4.9% compared to the year-ago period. In the third quarter, the company said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric. The company said it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth. For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase. Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase. headlines.title: Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts
headlines.summary: Investors will be looking for more insight into CEO Josh D'Amaro's strategy following several rounds of layoffs.
headlines.article_text: Disney (DIS) earnings Q4 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Disney topped Wall Street estimates for revenue and earnings per share for its fiscal fourth quarter. It's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029 via measures that include layoffs, CFO Hugh Johnston told CNBC. The company's results were once again boosted by strength in its streaming and parks divisions. In this article DIS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:20 02:20 Disney tops estimates on revenue, EPS in fourth-quarter earnings Squawk Box Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and announced it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029. Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month . Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs." Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy." "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he said. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth." The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026. The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%. Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks. "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston said. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded." The company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July. Here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3 , compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.77 adjusted vs. $1.67 expected Revenue : $25.95 billion vs. $25.18 billion expected Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77. The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions. Strength in parks Disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion. The division is already a top performer for the company, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year. While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston said. Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney. Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the Monsters, Inc.-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027. "Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he said. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits." The company expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March. Sports, streaming and entertainment Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion. Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said. The segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the company saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5." Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year. The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion. Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue. The company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the New Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61. Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026. Tech and AI D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer . "Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro said on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses." Disney announced a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models. D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier. "There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he said. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that plans and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World." headlines.article_text: Ex-Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Isomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised $5 billion. AI labs and investors are funnelling resources and cash into tools looking to use AI to develop new medicines. Isomorphic's round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab. Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis speaks at the 2026 Google I/O technology developer conference in Mountain View, California, May 19, 2026. Karl Mondon | Afp | Getty Images Isomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised a $5 billion Series C, the company said on Tuesday. Isomorphic's round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab, which he co-founded before the Big Tech giant acquired it in 2014. The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with investment from Alphabet , Google's parent. The fresh funds will help fund the design and development of new medicines using AI. Drug discovery startups have seen record funding poured into them by investors in 2026 as companies look to capitalize on advances in AI. OpenAI and Anthropic have also been investing in tools to develop new medicines using the technology. Hassabis has been CEO of Isomorphic Labs since the startup spun out of DeepMind in 2021. "When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI," said Hassabis. "This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients," he added. Isomorphic is building a proprietary drug design engine and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI, which it says will help it deliver the next generation of medicines. Anthropic announced it was launching an AI drug discovery program in June and OpenAI partnered with Novo Nordisk in April. Drug discovery startups have raised $23.2 billion in 2026, according to deal-counting platform Dealroom, a record figure. Isomorphic last raised in May, with a $2.1 billion Series B.
